question: How can a model show 94% overall accuracy while making wrong decisions for nearly one in three members of a small subgroup?
expected_answer_notes: The largest segment's 96% accuracy dominates the average, while a subgroup representing 6% of volume has only 71% accuracy; slice performance by segment to expose it.
system_answer: The reported 94% overall accuracy is an aggregate average (a weighted mean across subpopulations), and averages conceal localized subgroup failures. [S1][S2] The largest segment accounts for most of the volume and exhibits high accuracy (96%), which pulls the overall average up on its own. [S1] A small subgroup representing 6% of total volume can experience an accuracy of 71% (meaning roughly one in three customers receives a wrong decision) without shifting the headline metric. [S1][S2] Uncovering this failure requires slicing—evaluating performance separately by segment, geography, channel, language, or device. [S1][S2] A key limitation of slicing is that it only reveals disparities across attributes that evaluators specifically think to slice by. [S1][S2]

question: What three conditions together create the 'lethal trifecta' for prompt injection in an agent?
expected_answer_notes: The agent can read private data, consume untrusted content, and communicate externally; removing one leg breaks the trifecta.
system_answer: The lethal trifecta consists of three conditions: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and external communications (a way to send things out). [S1][S2] Private data refers to what the model is able to read; removing this leg leaves a safe but pointless assistant. [S1] Untrusted content refers to text not written by the system/developer (such as retrieval, browsing, or inbound mail), which typically constitutes the core product itself. [S1] External comms provides a mechanism to send data out; removing this leg converts the agent into a drafter. [S1] Holding all three legs creates a serious prompt injection vulnerability, while removing any single leg eliminates the trifecta condition. [S1][S2] The design target is holding at most two legs without a human in the loop, or alternatively narrowing the external destination rather than removing it entirely. [S1]

question: A manager cites the 55% versus 20% workflow-redesign figures as proof that redesign causes high AI performance. What is the flaw in that conclusion?
expected_answer_notes: The figures are cross-sectional correlation, not causal proof; prior organisational capability or earlier success could drive both, and longitudinal or natural-experiment evidence would be needed.
system_answer: The 55% versus 20% finding is derived from a cross-sectional survey, which represents a correlation and cannot establish causation. [S1][S2] Redesign causing performance is only one of three rival explanations that fit the survey gap. [S1][S2] A second explanation is that organizational capability causes both: firms capable of redesigning workflows already possess cross-functional authority, documented processes, and disruption tolerance, which predict success in any major program. [S1][S3] A third explanation is reverse causality (success causes redesign), where early wins generate the political capital and budget required to attempt structural change. [S1][S3] Separating these causal directions requires longitudinal data on the same firms or a natural experiment holding prior capability constant, neither of which currently exists. [S1][S3] Managers should hold the causal claim loosely rather than treating the 55% versus 20% gap as a proven lever. [S1][S3]

question: An organisation wants AI to produce a new score for something it has never measured before. What must it have to make that score credible, and what mistake remains possible?
expected_answer_notes: It needs an observable proxy and a calibration set with known truth; even then, an uncertain estimate may wrongly be treated as a fact.
system_answer: Creating a new score for something not previously measured represents Archetype B: manufacturing a measurement that did not exist. [S1][S2] To make the measurement possible and credible, the organisation must have an observable proxy that correlates with the thing it wants to measure. [S1] It must also have a calibration set where the ground truth is known. [S1] Even when built, a key failure mode is that the resulting estimate gets read as a fact. [S1] A related mistake is that while uncertainty is published, it never survives to the headline. [S1]

question: If OpenAI's board legally had the votes to remove its CEO in 2023, why did that legal power fail to settle the contest?
expected_answer_notes: Practical leverage lay outside the board: employees could leave, Microsoft could withhold compute or offer staff a landing place, and investors could pull a near-closing tender offer.
system_answer: The board's formal legal authority was never in doubt: four directors were legally sufficient to remove the CEO without cause by majority, and an independent review by WilmerHale confirmed the prior board acted within its broad discretion. [S1] Legal power failed to settle the contest because formal rights and actual power did not overlap: every formal power sat with the board, whereas every practical power sat outside it. [S1][S2] Actual control resided in the practical ability to withhold critical assets that could not be replaced quickly, none of which was governed by or included in the governance documents. [S1][S3] The employees held actual power because they could leave and take the company's only asset with them. [S1][S3] Microsoft held actual power outside the governance structure through its ability to supply or withhold compute, and as a shareholder offering ~770 staff a landing place within 48 hours. [S1][S2][S3] Investors possessed actual leverage through their ability to withdraw a tender-offer valuation that was only days from closing. [S1][S2]
